title: How Far Is Far?
sub: Grades 5–8 Math · Our Incredible Moon and Another Earth · Rates, scale and very large numbers
objective: Students will take the exhibition’s numbers, from the speed of Voyager 1 to the distance of the super-Earth HD 20794 d, and use rates, unit conversion and estimation to check the poster’s claim that the journey would take *hundreds of thousands of years*. At higher levels they will write the distances in scientific notation and shrink them to a scale they can picture.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Numbers this large stop meaning anything unless we can check them and picture them. A careful estimate is how a scientist, or a reader, knows whether to believe a claim.

items.text: use a rate to find a distance: miles per hour, to miles per day, to miles per year
items.question: use a rate to find a distance traveled?

items.text: convert between units of time and distance: light-years to light-days
items.question: convert light-years to light-days?

items.text: estimate with very large numbers, and check a claim made with them
items.question: estimate with very large numbers, and check a claim?

items.text: write very large numbers in scientific notation and use a scale to make them imaginable
items.question: use scientific notation and a scale to make a huge distance imaginable?

materials: Calculators for the Red level; paper for working
Page 3 of this plan (the answer key); differentiated handouts, one per student
connection: **On the posters:** *Our Incredible Moon* gives the Moon’s distance and drift, the Apollo samples and the temperatures; *Another Earth* gives Voyager 1 and HD 20794 d. In **Under the Microscope**, the lens buttons multiply: a 10× eyepiece over a 40× objective makes 400×.

steps.title: Still traveling
script: Play the Voyager sound. *“This spacecraft left Earth in 1977. It is still traveling, at nearly 38,000 miles an hour. How far do you think it has gone?”* Take guesses.

screen.question: Voyager 1 left Earth in 1977. How far do you think it has gone?

steps.purpose: Wonder at the speed and the distance before any numbers are worked.
students: Guess: how far has Voyager 1 traveled since 1977?

steps.title: The claim
script: Then read the poster: *“Even once we find a planet like HD 20794 d, traveling there would be extremely difficult. The planet is 20 light-years away, and with current technology, it would take hundreds of thousands of years to reach it.”* Students write a guess: thousands of years, hundreds of thousands, or millions? *“By the end of the lesson, you will check it.”*

screen.text: Even once we find a planet like HD 20794 d, traveling there would be extremely difficult. The planet is 20 light-years away, and with current technology, it would take hundreds of thousands of years to reach it.

steps.purpose: Meet the claim the lesson will check.
students: Write your guess before we work it out.

steps.title: Voyager’s light-day
script: **A rate, step by step.** Voyager 1 cruises at nearly 38,000 miles per hour. Per day: 38,000 × 24 = 912,000 miles. Per year: 912,000 × 365 ≈ 333 million miles. From 1977 to 2026 is 49 years: 333 million × 49 ≈ 16 billion miles. The poster says Voyager takes almost 50 years, until November 2026, to travel one **light-day**, about 16 billion miles: the distance light travels in a day. Our working agrees.

examples.title: One day
steps: Voyager 1 cruises at nearly **38,000 miles per hour**.

steps.purpose: Use a rate, step by step, to reach one light-day.

steps.title: Check the claim
script: **Convert, then estimate.** HD 20794 d is about 20 light-years away: 20 × 365 = 7,300 light-days, the number the poster gives. At almost 50 years for each light-day: 7,300 × 50 = 365,000 years. The claim, *hundreds of thousands of years*, holds.

examples.title: Light-years to light-days
steps: HD 20794 d is about **20 light-years** away.

examples.title: At Voyager’s speed
steps: Voyager takes almost **50 years** for each light-day.

examples.title: Check the claim
steps: The poster says *hundreds of thousands of years*.

steps.purpose: Convert units, estimate, and judge the poster’s claim.

steps.title: How far, in light-days?
script: **One unit.** Put four distances in light-days on the chart: the Moon (238,855 miles, a tiny fraction of one), Voyager 1, Proxima Centauri b (4.2 light-years) and HD 20794 d.

screen.caption: How far, in light-days? (one light-day is about 16 billion miles)

steps.purpose: Compare four distances in one unit.
students: Which is nearest? Which is farthest?
Work out Proxima Centauri b in light-days.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three use the exhibition’s own numbers; the answer key is page 3.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Guided steps: Voyager’s miles in a day, light-years to light-days, the Moon’s drift over 10 and 100 years, and the Moon’s temperature swing on a number line.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Voyager per year and since 1977, check the poster’s claim, the Moon’s drift in centimeters, the Apollo samples per sample, and the temperature swing in °F and °C.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Scientific notation for the distance to HD 20794 d, the speed needed to arrive in 100 years, a scale model with the Moon at 1 cm, and the microscope’s magnification.

steps.purpose: Practice rates, conversions and estimates at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use the exhibition’s own numbers.

steps.title: Exit ticket
script: *1. Proxima Centauri b, the closest known exoplanet, is 4.2 light-years away. About how many light-days is that?* (4.2 × 365 ≈ 1,533.) *2. At Voyager’s speed, about how many years would the trip take?* (1,533 × 50 ≈ 77,000 years.)
